overview: This file documents U.S. occupation authorities’ evolving treatment of Japan’s postwar telephone system, especially the compulsory purchase of 36,000-yen government bonds by new subscribers and the speculative private market in transferable “telephone rights.” A September 1948 despatch questions official claims that the bond merely covered installation costs, characterizing it instead as a forced loan or revenue measure to expand the network, while an enclosed SCAP letter explains its legal and financial basis. A January 1949 despatch and its enclosures record SCAPIN 1964, which sought to suppress speculation and the resale or rental of government telephone service after February 15, 1949, release reserved equipment, impose a three-month limit on approved applications, and preserve only limited transferability for pre-existing rights.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 579 on the Japanese Telephone Bond Law
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a change in occupation policy toward foreign residents’ purchase of compulsory Japanese telephone bonds and evaluates the bond as a revenue-raising measure.
subfiles.summary: The Acting Political Adviser forwards an August 18 GHQ letter clarifying that foreign commercial residents no longer need prior headquarters consent to buy the bond required for telephone installation. Although the Civil Communications Section describes the bond as a means of meeting installation costs, the Mission argues that the 36,000-yen payment, imposed in addition to installation fees and sometimes after circuit rights have been bought from a broker, functions chiefly as a forced loan or tax to maintain and expand the system. The Mission suggests that foreign traders would prefer higher monthly charges comparable to those in the United States over an initial outlay of roughly $150, while occupation communications officials maintain that rates have already risen nearly fiftyfold.

subfiles.title: GHQ letter to the Eighth Army on the Telephone Bond Law
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers; signed by J. F. Bradshaw by command of General MacArthur
subfiles.about: Explains the terms, financial rationale, rates, and licensing implications of Japan’s compulsory telephone-bond system.
subfiles.summary: The letter states that applicants for telephone service must purchase a 36,000-yen government bond, redeemable after fifteen years and paying four percent interest, with exceptions for the Japanese government and occupation forces. It argues that severe inflation has made the former installation and registration fees inadequate to finance new facilities and compares Japanese monthly charges with U.S. rates. It further rules that compulsory bond purchases by licensed commercial entrants are costs of doing business rather than prohibited yen investments. Foreign nationals and stateless personnel employed by occupation forces may use an existing priority procedure, but must pay for their own bonds.

subfiles.title: Partial duplicate of GHQ letter on the Telephone Bond Law
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Preserves the first page of a duplicate copy of the August 18 GHQ explanation of the telephone-bond system.
subfiles.summary: This page duplicates the opening portion of the GHQ letter enclosed with Despatch No. 579. It describes the compulsory 36,000-yen, fifteen-year, four-percent telephone bond, the effect of inflation on earlier installation and registration fees, and comparative monthly rates in Tokyo and the United States. The surviving copy ends after paragraph four and does not include the licensing interpretation and signature found on pages 3–4.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 55 on speculation in telephone rights
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards and analyzes a SCAP directive and press release intended to restrict speculation and profiteering in Japanese telephone rights and service.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that SCAPIN 1964 prohibits transfers of telephone contracts, agreements, and registrations issued on or after February 15, 1949, limits approvals to applications that can be filled within three months, and directs the release of reserve equipment. It also prohibits future recipients from reselling, subletting, or renting government telecommunications service, while allowing older rights to be transferred when the associated service is transferred simultaneously to the same party. The Political Adviser notes that the accompanying press-release headline overstates the directive’s reach because pre-February 15 rights remain transferable. The despatch also highlights a shift in official explanation of the 36,000-yen bond, now described as assistance in financing additional plant rather than direct reimbursement of installation expenses.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1964: Treatment of Telephone Rights and Prohibition of Resale
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers; signed by R. M. Levy
subfiles.about: Directs the Japanese government to end recognition of newly transferred telephone rights, restrict applications, release facilities, and prohibit resale or rental of public telecommunications service.
subfiles.summary: SCAPIN 1964 orders that contracts and registrations issued from February 15, 1949 onward bind only their original recipients and possess no transferable property value, while leaving previously issued rights outside that prohibition. Applications are to be approved only when service can reasonably be supplied within three months, and unused facilities must be made available under existing priority rules. Equipment reserved for holders of older rights is protected only until April 1, 1949. The directive prohibits resale, subletting, rental, and other transfers of service, subject to limited exceptions for simultaneous transfers of older rights and service and for government-approved special services such as semipublic telephones, hotel exchanges, and toll facilities.

subfiles.title: Press release: “Direct Japanese to Abolish Private Speculation in Telephones”
subfiles.from: Public Information Office, General Headquarters, Far East Command
subfiles.about: Publicizes SCAP’s restrictions on telephone-right speculation and explains the historical development and economic effects of the private market.
subfiles.summary: The release traces transferable telephone rights to Japan’s early telephone system, when high registration and installation fees created a permanent, marketable entitlement to service. Scarcity turned these rights into assets resembling stock certificates, reportedly selling for as much as 55,000 yen in the Tokyo area, while telephone rentals could reach ten or twelve times the legal service rate. It explains that postwar fee freezes reduced installation and registration charges to 1,800 yen and that future subscribers would instead pay the low fee and purchase 36,000 yen in interest-bearing government bonds to help finance additional plant. New service would be allocated by priority and could be moved by the subscriber but neither sold to another party nor retained as an asset while the service was rented out.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how a basic public utility became a speculative property market amid postwar scarcity, inflation, and war damage. Its successive documents expose a revealing change in official rhetoric: the 36,000-yen bond is first justified as covering installation costs but later described more candidly as a forced loan for system expansion. The bundle also documents the tension between occupation reformers’ egalitarian language, the protection of vested pre-1949 rights, and the practical need to finance reconstruction without raising already inflated monthly rates.
